Country Life also reports a separate annexe, mature formal gardens and a rear swimming-pool extension made almost entirely of glass. articles.title: We Love This Listing: Shrubs Wood’s Remarkable Modernist Inheritance
articles.deck: A Buckinghamshire house where Mendelsohn and Chermayeff’s architecture, original furniture and garden history make a compelling whole.
paragraphs: A partnership preserved

Some houses deserve attention for the ideas they embody rather than their scale alone. Shrubs Wood, in Chalfont St Giles, is one such prospect. Country Life identifies it as a collaboration between Erich Mendelsohn and Serge Chermayeff, built in 1933–1934 and now Grade II*-listed. For us, that architectural authorship is the starting point of its appeal.
Concrete with a flourish

Country Life reports that the reinforced-concrete construction enabled large rooms, uninterrupted floor space and picture windows, alongside a quadrant-curve staircase. That combination is particularly engaging: structural ambition paired with a softer geometric gesture. The staircase offers a compelling counterpoint to the house’s largely rectangular plan.
More than an architectural shell

According to Country Life, the house contains 3,735 sq ft of internal space, with separate living and dining rooms and six first-floor bedrooms. The publication also reports that much of the furniture was designed specifically for the house by its architects. That continuity gives the interiors significance beyond a collection of period-compatible pieces.
A second creative chapter

Country Life credits Bridget D’Oyly Carte, who moved here in 1949, with transforming the five-acre grounds into gardens that are locally listed. Our reading of Shrubs Wood’s appeal is therefore twofold: a notable Modernist collaboration, complemented by a later landscape legacy rather than defined by architecture alone.

paragraphs: A different kind of grandeur

Baltersan’s appeal is not a finished interior but the architecture that remains. Details worth protecting

Country Life reports that Baltersan is Category A listed. Citing selling agent Galbraith, it describes moulded stonework, intricate doorways and fireplaces, carved stone waterspouts and a secret chamber. For us, those particulars are the real draw: the castle’s character resides in specific surviving craftsmanship, not just its scale.
An artist’s record

Country Life also reports that Charles Rennie Mackintosh sketched the castle’s details, with the resulting drawings held in Glasgow’s Hunterian Art Gallery. That connection adds another dimension to its appeal: Baltersan is both a surviving structure and a subject of architectural study.
The reality behind the romance

The distinction matters: Country Life says the walls remain close to their original height, but the floors have gone. This is a conservation proposition, not a ready-made mansion. Our editorial interest lies in that tension between substantial architectural survival and the considerable work still ahead.

articles.deck: In Country Life, garden designer James Alexander-Sinclair recalls the six-bedroom country house he built within a former farmyard—and later sold.

Alexander-Sinclair describes finding a concrete courtyard with tumble-down barns beside his parents-in-law’s home. The appeal here is the transformation: an agricultural site became the setting for a family house, with proximity to grandparents helping to shape the decision.
Six bedrooms, one clear footprint

According to his account, the new house was L-shaped, with six bedrooms, all within the original courtyard. That relationship between a substantial house and an existing footprint offers a more particular architectural story than size alone.
Salvage and compromise

He reports dismantling the old structures to reuse their bricks and roof slates, although the gathered slates were stolen. He also recalls economising on radiators after the house exceeded their budget. Those admissions give the project a refreshingly unvarnished character: ambition came with practical trade-offs.
The connection beyond the wall

One detail stands out in his recollection: a gap in the garden wall allowed access to his wife’s parents’ house and the woods. He says the family sold after the children left home. This is a retrospective portrait, not a claim of current availability; its strongest theme is a home shaped around a particular chapter of family life.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A 1911 Venice Beach House With Layers of Character
articles.deck: A triple-lot estate near the beach pairs a boarding-house past with timber ceilings, distinctive fireplaces and generous gathering spaces.
paragraphs: A history beyond the headline

According to Robb Report, this Venice Beach property was built in 1911 for Warren Wilson, founder of the Los Angeles Daily Journal. It later became a boarding house whose guests included Charlie Chaplin and Abbot Kinney. Those connections are compelling, but the architectural continuity makes the stronger editorial case.
Character in the materials

Robb Report identifies retained hardwood floors, wood-beam ceilings on both levels, and decorative tile and brick fireplaces. We love the combination: several distinct materials carrying the history, rather than one period detail doing all the work.
Rooms with individual identities

The publication reports nine bedrooms and seven bathrooms, describing a plaid-wallpapered bedroom with a private balcony and another bedroom paired with a navy-blue sitting room. The appeal here is individuality rather than uniformity—a fitting quality for a house with such a layered past.
Shared spaces, inside and out

Robb Report describes a wood-paneled living area with a working wood-burning fireplace, a dining banquette curving into a bay window, and a brick garden walkway connecting a deck and covered porch. To us, these varied gathering spaces are the feature’s quiet counterweight to its famous-name history.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A London Water Tower With a New Perspective
articles.deck: Victorian brickwork, a glass-and-steel addition and a former water tank turned lookout give this London conversion its distinctive architectural rhythm.
paragraphs: Infrastructure, Reconsidered

According to Robb Report, this tower was built in the 1860s to supply the nearby Lambeth Workhouse and converted into a roughly 4,500-square-foot residence in 2011. Its appeal lies in that dramatic change of purpose: an imposing piece of civic infrastructure rethought at a domestic scale.
A Deliberate Contrast

Robb Report describes Venetian Gothic brickwork paired with an ultramodern glass-and-steel extension called the Cube. Its ground floor contains an open-plan kitchen and dining room alongside a reception room with full-height sliding glass doors. Architecturally, the contrast is more compelling than an attempt to make the addition disappear.
A Home That Climbs

The report identifies an original York stone staircase connecting the floors, plus a separate added elevator tower. Five bedrooms and four bathrooms occupy the tower. That vertical arrangement suggests a different domestic rhythm from a sprawling mansion, with movement between levels central to the design.
The Tank Becomes the Destination

At the top, Robb Report places the Prospect Room inside the original cast-iron water tank, with windows on all four sides and views including the London Eye. This is the conversion’s strongest idea: giving the tower’s defining industrial component a new role rather than treating it as a relic.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Bulford Mill Keeps Its Working History in View
articles.deck: Country Life’s account of this Essex mill conversion reveals retained machinery, a five-storey layout and a top floor dedicated to music and games.
paragraphs: Machinery, not memorabilia

A conversion is more interesting when its past helps shape its character. Country Life describes Bulford Mill as Grade II-listed, with restored milling equipment appearing throughout the home. For us, retaining that machinery offers something decoration alone cannot: a direct connection between the rooms and their original purpose.
History with an important distinction

Country Life places Bulford Mill near Cressing and traces the site’s milling history across 1,000 years. That should not be confused with the age of the present building. Its account describes a former fulling mill, later converted to grind corn and barley around 250 years ago, when it was apparently substantially rebuilt.
An expansive vertical plan

According to Country Life, the main house exceeds 6,300 sq ft across five storeys, with all five bedrooms on the second floor. The top floor contains a games and music room spanning the building. Our favourite aspect of that arrangement is the prominence given to shared pursuits: recreation gets a whole level, rather than a leftover corner.
Water as context

Country Life reports river views and five acres of grounds visible from every room. To us, those outlooks give the conversion’s industrial story a landscape setting, connecting domestic life with the resource that explains the mill’s presence.

Country Life reports about 134 acres of gardens and grounds, with woodland, rhododendrons and azaleas to the north and more formal gardens to the south. Country Life dates Havilland Hall’s completion to 1830 and places it in Guernsey’s Vauquiedor valley near St Peter Port. The publication compares its neo-Classical frontage with the north façade of the White House, citing four pillars, a pediment and iron balconies. The architectural appeal lies in that disciplined composition, rather than the famous resemblance alone.
Space beyond ceremony

According to Country Life, a vestibule opens into a grand hallway with a curving staircase and galleried landing. Alongside the drawing and formal dining rooms, the publication describes a snug with a separate bar. That contrast is compelling: a house with ceremonial scale also makes room for a less formal register.
An extended southern edge

Country Life reports an orangery stretching more than 50 feet along the house’s south side, plus a modern addition containing an indoor pool with a glass ceiling, gym and spa rooms. Editorially, the orangery is the standout counterpoint to the formal frontage—a long, light-oriented space rather than another statement reception room.
An estate in several parts

The publication describes 80 acres encompassing formal gardens, lawns and woodland, alongside an area called ‘the village’ with five separate cottages and other estate buildings. That arrangement gives Havilland Hall a broader identity than its mansion alone: the interest is in the relationship between a commanding main house and its smaller-scale surroundings.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A Wiltshire Farmhouse Rethinking What Lies Behind Tradition
articles.deck: At West Swainsford Farm near Mere, a reported 3,000sq ft farmhouse pairs traditional lime-rendered design with hemp-based construction and an ambitious energy specification.
paragraphs: A farmhouse with a different brief

Country Life reports that the farmhouse at West Swainsford Farm, near Mere in Wiltshire, is a collaboration between Hemspan and the Duchy of Cornwall. The article quotes Duchy sustainability officer Sam Henderson describing the 3,000sq ft project as a research and development exercise. For us, that experimental brief is its defining attraction.
Traditional does not mean conventional

Architect Alex Hibbert-Job tells Country Life that the house was designed as a traditional, lime-rendered Duchy farmhouse rather than a modernist structure. Our interest lies in that distinction: architectural familiarity need not rule out a different approach to construction.
The work behind the walls

According to Country Life, the timber-frame construction uses a panel system manufactured off-site. Hibbert-Job describes its intended performance as bordering on passive-house thermal efficiency. That is a reported design assessment, rather than a claim of passive-house certification.
An energy strategy worth examining

Country Life lists a 13-kilowatt solar system, battery storage, an air-source heat pump and mechanical ventilation with heat recovery. It also describes an underground-air Canadian well system. Editorially, the compelling idea is the combination: this is a farmhouse whose interest extends beyond its outward style to how its systems are intended to work together.

articles.deck: The roof at 427 Washington Street covers the building’s footprint. A former industrial neighbourhood makes an unusually good backdrop for a garden.
paragraphs: The block from above

Robb Report puts it at roughly 4,600 square feet. A water tower shares the roof with raised planting beds and places to sit. The neighbouring rooftops give the garden a distinctly New York horizon.
The floor below

Downstairs, the apartment takes a different approach to the same view. Eighteen windows face in four directions. A 48-foot great room accommodates both dining and lounging, and an alcove beside the dining area has room for a grand piano. The two bedrooms are part of the current arrangement. articles.title: We Love This Listing: Two pavilions frame the garden at Stoke Park
articles.deck: At Stoke Bruerne in Northamptonshire, matching buildings on either side of a pool lead remarkably different lives.
paragraphs: Reading the garden front

Look across the water in the Strutt & Parker photograph and the two stone pavilions appear to balance each other perfectly. The house where a family would spend most of its time sits farther back. Country Life featured this 113-acre estate on November 21, reporting a guide price of £5.25 million. The River Tove marks its southern edge.
A library and a chapel

The west pavilion once held a library and later served as a ballroom. More recently it has hosted weddings. Across the garden, the east pavilion began as a chapel and now contains a two-bedroom residence. Those histories explain how one building could host a crowd while its near twin could accommodate someone for the night. Behind them, the four-bedroom Victorian house has its own connection with the grounds. Its library and study open to the garden, giving the family a quieter route outside.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: An Oxted shop counter stays put as the customers move out
articles.deck: At the former London Stores in Surrey, the old department store’s central stair still carries people between floors.
paragraphs: Where the shoppers went

Follow the broad wooden staircase through the centre of 79 High Street and it is easy to picture the building as a shop. T. Troughton London Stores once sold goods ranging from china to bed linen here in Oxted. Country Life featured its conversion into a five-bedroom house on November 13. John D Wood listed a guide price of £1.25 million. Two original counters remain, one on the ground floor and another on the first.
Life behind the counter

One counter now shares a thirty-foot sitting and dining room with exposed floorboards and wood panelling. It gives a visitor an immediate sense of scale. Imagine how much of a conventional living room would disappear beneath a shop fixture of that size. Upstairs, two bedrooms face the back garden. Delivery horses once occupied stables on that ground, close enough for a cart to carry purchases away from the shop.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Five concrete frames lift Lovell Beach House above the sand
articles.deck: At Newport Beach, R. M. Schindler arranged the living spaces around a two-storey view of the Pacific.
paragraphs: How to read the house from the street

Look for the gap beneath the upper rooms. R. M. Schindler carried the home on five concrete frames, raising the rooms where Philip and Leah Lovell spent their days above the sand. A tall grid of windows lets light into the double-height living room. The family could take in the Pacific from that room, then move up to the bedrooms along a projecting balcony. The Spaces reported an asking price of $18.8 million on November 12.
A coastal experiment revised

The house dates to 1926. In the original design, the sleeping porches were open to the air. Two years later Schindler enclosed them because the coastal fog made them too cold. Inside, a sofa and shelves he designed still give the dining and living areas their own boundaries. That piece of furniture solves at the scale of a room the same question the concrete frames address outside. What has to carry weight, and what can stay open?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: The Squirrel House keeps an art collector’s garden in view
articles.deck: A garden wall and a gallery wall share the light at Barbara Jakobson’s former East 74th Street home.
paragraphs: An invitation to look up

In the photograph of the living room, artwork reaches up one wall and a black grid divides the glass facing the garden. Through those panes a guest could keep an eye on the courtyard while talking to someone on the sofa. A skylight brings daylight in from another direction. It is easy to see how this room lent itself to conversation. The Spaces reported on November 20 that Christie’s International Real Estate had listed the townhouse for $8.995 million.
Spot the squirrels from the sidewalk

Collector Barbara Jakobson bought the house in 1965, nine years after architect John Kingsland enlarged it. Among the visitors she welcomed here were artist Jasper Johns and writer Philip Roth. The house has eight bedrooms across five storeys, but some of its most memorable art is visible without setting foot indoors. Bronze squirrels made by Jane Canfield accompany the red lacquered entrance doors. They explain the name by which neighbours came to know the place.

articles.deck: A stone wall marks the edge of a south-facing garden at this West Sussex house dating to 1694.
paragraphs: A view across the channel

Seen from the water, the Old Town Hall sits behind a low stone wall. The dormers break up a steep roof, and the colour of the stone repeats in the wall along the shore. The south-facing garden runs beside Bosham Channel, with paved terraces and enough lawn to enjoy the water from farther back. On November 16, The Spaces reported that Finlay Brewer was seeking offers above £3.25 million for the Grade II-listed house.
Which room gets the view

The dining room occupies a later extension with a vaulted ceiling. French doors open towards the water, giving the table a connection to the channel even when the garden is too cold for lunch. Older details survive elsewhere, including flagstone floors and a carved lintel above the inglenook. Five bedrooms fill the upper levels, while a separate staircase leads to an office. A flat above the detached garage provides another place to stay.

At the front, shuttered windows and a timber door face the village street. The back of the house has a more private outlook. Here the kitchen opens to a courtyard where vines shade a second place to cook. Three bedrooms occupy the upper floor, each with a bathroom. In one, the warm colour comes from the terracotta-toned floor beneath a freestanding tub.

For a visitor walking in from the street, the changes in texture offer a way to remember the rooms in a compact floor plan.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A window seat faces the Pacific in Carl Maston’s Faria Beach house
articles.deck: A 1984 commission on Ventura’s coast takes its cues from the small summer cabins that once stood along the beach.
paragraphs: A house seen from the sand

From the beach, slim uprights divide a long bank of glass, and a tree stands between the house and its rail. Those narrow divisions make sense from the other side of the windows. Maston designed a built-in seat where someone can look out at the Pacific without moving a chair into place. Tracy Susman commissioned the three-bedroom house in 1984. The Spaces reported its first offering for sale on November 10.
What survives of the original design

Across its 2,640 square feet, Maston used cedar, exposed beams, concrete and brick. The roof changes level, giving the timber-lined interior a shape beyond that of a simple seaside box. Photographer Julius Shulman recorded the house in 1985. Those early pictures provide an unusual reference for reading what has survived, from the original materials to pieces of furniture designed to stay in place. The feature photograph here is by Sterling Reed.

articles.deck: In northwest London, architect Peter Morris drew on a neighbourhood church and a honeymoon in Florida to design a house for his family.
paragraphs: A roofline you can trace with a finger

A row of pink arches climbs towards the middle of the frontage and drops again at the far end. Blue sky shows in the tall windows. The colour came from a trip Peter Morris and Emily Kennedy took to Miami, while the arch shape owes something to nearby St Martin’s Church. The couple bought a former vicarage here and redesigned the site as two adjoining homes. The Spaces featured Cloud House on November 23 and reported an asking price of £2.5 million.
Room for work and a bath under the sky

The ground floor puts Morris’s studio alongside the kitchen, living and dining areas. Cupboard edges are scalloped and the kitchen is striped, details close enough to touch after seeing the bigger curves from the pavement. There is a bedroom and bathroom on each of the next two floors. On the roof terrace, a bathtub takes the daily routine of bathing outdoors.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A glass winter garden opens the roof at Maison H
articles.deck: Bruno Albert put the living rooms upstairs in this Belgian house, where the slope brings the treetops close.
paragraphs: Looking up from the garden

From the grounds of Maison H, the roof looks almost big enough to be the house. One end opens into a rounded cage of glass, with an outdoor stair running down from it. In Esneux, architect Bruno Albert took advantage of the hillside by putting the private rooms on the lower level. A timber spiral staircase leads up to the kitchen, library and spaces for eating and sitting. The light from the winter garden reaches into those rooms.
Art built into the rooms

The house took shape between 1980 and 1985. Gérald Dederen contributed to the barrel vault over the shared spaces, while Léon Wuidar designed sliding panels with geometric patterns. Someone moving a panel changes the room and the artwork in the same gesture. Jean-Pierre Herzet’s sculptures extend that collaboration into the wooded grounds. The Spaces reported a €1.195 million asking price through ArchitectenWoning on November 24.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Schindler's Lovell Beach House comes up for sale
articles.deck: On the sand at Newport Beach, the 1926 house RM Schindler designed for Dr Philip Lovell is listed for $18.8 million. These photographs are of that house.
paragraphs: On the sand

The Spaces reported that the Lovell Beach House, designed by RM Schindler in 1926, is for sale for the first time in its history. It stands on the sand at Newport Beach and is listed for $18.8 million. The house has stayed in the same family since it was built for naturopath Dr Philip Lovell and his wife Leah.
The frame

Schindler set the house on five reinforced-concrete frames so the rooms look straight at the Pacific. A double-height living room faces the ocean through a wall of glass, and a cantilevered balcony connects four bedrooms above. Original Schindler furniture remains, including a built-in sofa and shelving between the living and dining rooms. Sleeping porches were enclosed by Schindler in 1928 after the coastal fog proved too cold.
The record

The house has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1974. The asking price and the photographs belong to the listing account published by The Spaces. Current availability is not independently confirmed.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A Cornish Lodge with Its Own Identity
articles.deck: Country Life’s account of The Lodge at Porthpean House reveals a compact coastal home with a thoughtfully divided plan.
paragraphs: The lodge, not the main house

Country Life identifies this property as the lodge in the grounds of Porthpean House, rather than the main house itself. That distinction is worth keeping centre stage: our interest lies in the smaller home’s own proportions and arrangement, not in borrowing grandeur from its neighbour.
An L-shaped starting point

According to the publication, The Lodge has an L-shaped plan, measures just over 1,000 square feet and contains three bedrooms and two bathrooms. To our minds, the interesting balance is between its modest overall size and the number of separate rooms—not a claim to sprawling country-house scale.
Together, and apart

Country Life also reports a large kitchen-diner and a separate sitting room. That is the layout detail we particularly like: cooking and dining share a setting, while sitting has a room of its own. The appeal is separation rather than an entirely open-plan arrangement.
A coastal connection

The beach is a few moments’ stroll away, Country Life reports, with St Austell a few minutes’ drive away. For us, that near-beach setting is the strongest thread in the story. It gives this compact lodge a coastal identity without requiring any claim to private shoreline.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: At Broadgate Farm, eight paddocks and two homes share ten acres
articles.deck: A farm track links this East Markham smallholding to the village bridlepath, while a second converted barn receives overnight guests.
paragraphs: Shelter in every field

Look beyond the gravel courtyard and you can see why the arrangement of the fields matters at Broadgate Farm. The ten acres are split into eight paddocks, each with its own shelter. A rider can follow the farm track out to a bridlepath leading to East Markham. Horse & Hound reports that permission has been granted for a full-sized riding arena. A buyer looking round today can inspect the fields and stables and decide where that next piece would fit.
What became of the barns

The main barn became a family home in 2020. Its kitchen shares an open room with the dining area, and a spiral stair goes up to a small library. The Old Dairy has a different role. Its five bedrooms have their own bathrooms, a practical arrangement for its use as holiday accommodation. Horse & Hound reported a £1.425 million asking price in its November 23 feature. articles.title: We Love This Listing: A tree sets the course for arrival at an Oakland Hills manor
articles.deck: At the Hillcrest Estates house on Skyline Boulevard, the drive circles a mature tree before it reaches the front door.
paragraphs: A tree at the front door

The open gates frame a broad tree in a ring of paving. Its crown spreads across the middle of the house, so it takes a moment to pick out the front door behind it. The wings on either side are easier to see. Their low eaves bring the scale of the building down at the courtyard edge, something that matters on a property large enough to have a six-car garage.
What fits behind the courtyard

The Week featured the six-bedroom Oakland house on November 23, reporting an asking price of $2.985 million. Built in 1993, the house takes advantage of its hillside setting with views across San Francisco Bay. A few steps down into the living room, a vaulted ceiling gives extra height above the fireplace and French doors. An apartment sits over the garage, giving someone on a longer stay a place of their own on the grounds. Want to see your property here?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: The pool follows a curve at Leuthold House in New Canaan
articles.deck: Allan Gelbin’s design sets glass, mahogany and sweeping rooflines among five acres of trees in Connecticut.
paragraphs: A curve seen from the water

At the edge of the swimming pool, look up. The broad roof bends above the upper windows, and its warm underside is visible from the terrace. A pale wall turns another corner below. Photographer Daniel Milstein’s view captures the echo between these lines and the curve of the pool. Allan Gelbin designed the two-storey house, completed in 1966. Frank Lloyd Wright was his mentor.
A landscape beyond the pool

The grounds have a second body of water, a pond supplied by a spring. A one-bedroom guest house stands on the five acres, which also hold about 150 specimen trees. Inside the main house, stretches of glass bring those plantings into the rooms, where mahogany contributes a warmer surface. Hobbs Inc. and JMK Architects restored the five-bedroom house in 2014. ELLE Decor reported the listing at $6.2 million through Douglas Elliman on November 20.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: The arches at the Cloisters trace a garden path in Palm Springs
articles.deck: Liberace’s former desert home began as a bed-and-breakfast. Its walls enclose a series of courtyards.
paragraphs: Reading the garden at dusk

In the listing photograph, the first things to catch the light are the palms. Then the illuminated arches draw the eye across the lawn to the house. This series of sheltered passages and courtyards explains the name the Cloisters. The estate began as a Spanish Colonial Revival bed-and-breakfast in the 1930s. Liberace bought it in the late 1960s and lived here until his death in 1987.
After the show

The pianist furnished his Palm Springs rooms with gold accents and the candelabras associated with his stage shows. Brett Waterman led a later update, with the emphasis shifting to handcrafted details. The half-acre grounds offer more than a pretty approach to the front door. A heated pool and spa give the gardens places to pause, with the San Jacinto Mountains in view. ELLE Decor reported an asking price of nearly $6.9 million on November 20.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: At Sword Gate House, the harbour comes into the dining room
articles.deck: A painted view of Charleston survives inside this early nineteenth-century house in the South of Broad neighbourhood.
paragraphs: An ironworker left the house its name

Start at the street, where Christopher Werner’s wrought-iron gates still mark the entrance. The gardens beyond occupy about an acre. Then look inside the dining room, where an original mural brings a view of the historic harbour to the table. Between them, the gates and the painting preserve two very different ways the city figures in the design of a single address.
A house scaled for gatherings

A three-level piazza gives the house several vantage points over the grounds, while the ballroom provides space to gather indoors. In Nick Cann’s interior photograph, a piano stands beside tall windows. Dark walls throw the pale shutters and their deep surrounds into relief. ELLE Decor described the preserved millwork as part of interior designer Cortney Bishop’s renovation and reported a $35 million asking price through Maison Real Estate on November 20.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: A Sedona neighbourhood’s old water tank now holds wine
articles.deck: At La Aguilera on Cibola Drive, two houses share an unusual piece of the neighbourhood’s history.
paragraphs: A second use for a steel tank

Before anyone thought of storing wine here, the tank at La Aguilera supplied water to homes in Cibola Hills. It went into service in the late 1950s and remained in use into the 1990s. Fancy Pants Homes reports that the owners later bought the empty tank from the water company for five dollars. Converting it took considerably more work. Between October 2009 and June 2010 the steel shell became a cellar and tasting room with space for around 1,600 bottles.
Outside the cellar

The listing covers two residences at 25 and 55 Cibola Drive. In the broker’s photograph, the terrace walls echo the red rock beyond the trees. The flat roofs step down the slope, and the decks have clear views into the woodland. Only a visitor who knew the history would think to look for a piece of the neighbourhood’s former water system on these grounds. Want to see your property here?

item.title: This London Water Tower Has Been Turned Into a Contemporary $3.7 Million Residence
item.summary: Dating to the 1860s, the original structure has been paired with a glass and steel extension.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A London Water Tower With a New Perspective
illustrationDraft.deck: Victorian brickwork, a glass-and-steel addition and a former water tank turned lookout give this London conversion its distinctive architectural rhythm.
paragraphs: Infrastructure, Reconsidered

According to Robb Report, this tower was built in the 1860s to supply the nearby Lambeth Workhouse and converted into a roughly 4,500-square-foot residence in 2011. Its appeal lies in that dramatic change of purpose: an imposing piece of civic infrastructure rethought at a domestic scale.
A Deliberate Contrast

Robb Report describes Venetian Gothic brickwork paired with an ultramodern glass-and-steel extension called the Cube. Its ground floor contains an open-plan kitchen and dining room alongside a reception room with full-height sliding glass doors. Architecturally, the contrast is more compelling than an attempt to make the addition disappear.
A Home That Climbs

The report identifies an original York stone staircase connecting the floors, plus a separate added elevator tower. Five bedrooms and four bathrooms occupy the tower. That vertical arrangement suggests a different domestic rhythm from a sprawling mansion, with movement between levels central to the design.
The Tank Becomes the Destination

At the top, Robb Report places the Prospect Room inside the original cast-iron water tank, with windows on all four sides and views including the London Eye. This is the conversion’s strongest idea: giving the tower’s defining industrial component a new role rather than treating it as a relic.

item.title: This $13.9 Million Venice Beach Compound Has Ties to Charlie Chaplin
item.summary: The nine-bedroom home once served as a boarding house that attracted the likes of Charlie Chaplin.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A 1911 Venice Beach House With Layers of Character
illustrationDraft.deck: A triple-lot estate near the beach pairs a boarding-house past with timber ceilings, distinctive fireplaces and generous gathering spaces.
paragraphs: A history beyond the headline

According to Robb Report, this Venice Beach property was built in 1911 for Warren Wilson, founder of the Los Angeles Daily Journal. It later became a boarding house whose guests included Charlie Chaplin and Abbot Kinney. Those connections are compelling, but the architectural continuity makes the stronger editorial case.
Character in the materials

Robb Report identifies retained hardwood floors, wood-beam ceilings on both levels, and decorative tile and brick fireplaces. We love the combination: several distinct materials carrying the history, rather than one period detail doing all the work.
Rooms with individual identities

The publication reports nine bedrooms and seven bathrooms, describing a plaid-wallpapered bedroom with a private balcony and another bedroom paired with a navy-blue sitting room. The appeal here is individuality rather than uniformity—a fitting quality for a house with such a layered past.
Shared spaces, inside and out

Robb Report describes a wood-paneled living area with a working wood-burning fireplace, a dining banquette curving into a bay window, and a brick garden walkway connecting a deck and covered porch. To us, these varied gathering spaces are the feature’s quiet counterweight to its famous-name history.

item.title: This $14 Million Equestrian Estate Sits Within a Double-Gated Orange County Community
item.summary: The three-acre spread, located in the exclusive Los Ranchos Estates, features a four-stall barn and riding arena.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Three-Acre Equestrian Estate in Coto de Caza
illustrationDraft.deck: Horse facilities anchor this Orange County estate, where Robb Report describes a renovated main residence, separate guest house and generous spaces for gathering.
paragraphs: The Horses Come First

According to Robb Report, the three-acre property includes a four-stall barn with a tack room, office and saloon, alongside a riding arena and three pastures. That combination gives the equestrian identity substance: this is not simply a large house borrowing ranch style.
Rustic, Without Being One-Note

Robb Report dates the original construction to 1981 and notes subsequent renovations. Its description of the 8,400-square-foot main residence pairs cathedral ceilings and exposed beams with a neutral palette. The appeal is that balance: substantial architectural gestures, with finishes that sound comparatively restrained.
Room for Different Gatherings

The publication reports dual stone-top kitchen islands, a living-room wet bar and a temperature-controlled wine cellar with approximately 1,700-bottle capacity and a dedicated tasting room. Read together, these suggest several distinct settings for hosting, rather than one oversized entertaining space expected to do everything.
A Separate Place to Stay

Robb Report also describes a one-bedroom guest house with an open-plan living room, dining room and kitchen, plus access to a sauna and steam room. Editorially, that separate accommodation is a compelling counterpoint to the main residence’s scale: room for company without making every gathering communal.

item.title: This Olson Kundig-Designed Home Frames Hawaii’s Rugged Landscape
item.summary: The 6,500-square-foot residence on the Big Island's Kona Coast is made up of a series of glass-walled pavilions set within a courtyard garden.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Kona Coast Home Composed Around Lava and Courtyards
illustrationDraft.deck: Olson Kundig’s pavilion-style residence pairs ocean-facing outdoor spaces with a remarkably deliberate approach to privacy, shade and volcanic terrain.
paragraphs: A collection of smaller worlds

According to Robb Report, Olson Kundig designed this 6,500-square-foot Kona Coast residence as flat-roofed pavilions arranged around gardens and courtyards. The appeal is architectural rather than simply expansive: breaking the home into separate structures makes the spaces between buildings feel as important as the rooms themselves.
Views that unfold

Robb Report describes a nine-foot-tall slatted wood screen concealing the front door, followed by a view across the courtyard toward a cinder cone and the ocean beyond. That sequence is the compelling idea here: the landscape becomes a gradual reveal, rather than a single panorama delivered at the threshold.
Privacy with an outdoor connection

The primary suite occupies its own building, linked to the main house by a covered walkway, the publication reports. Each bedroom also opens onto a private courtyard with an outdoor shower. To us, those individual outdoor spaces are a particularly thoughtful counterpoint to the shared gathering areas.
Materials in conversation with the site

Robb Report identifies concrete walls, wood ceilings, cedar screens and basalt stone floors, with deep roof overhangs providing shade. Our favorite aspect is the restrained material vocabulary: it offers a way to read the architecture alongside the lava landscape without treating that rugged setting as mere scenery.

item.title: Clive Davis’s Park Avenue Penthouse Lists for $11 Million
item.summary: The late music mogul's two-tiered aerie at The Ritz Tower in Manhattan's Midtown East neighborhood is now available for the first time.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Park Avenue Penthouse Composed for Company
illustrationDraft.deck: Clive Davis’s Ritz Tower duplex pairs a nearly 48-foot great room with a screening room and a distinctly two-level approach to entertaining, according to Robb Report.
paragraphs: Two Apartments, One Ambitious Home

Robb Report traces the penthouse’s creation to Davis’s purchase of a full-floor apartment in 1985 and the unit below in 1989, followed by a collaboration with designers Vicente Wolf and Robert Metzger. Our take: the combination gives this home a more interesting premise than size alone.
A Great Room with a Musical Past

According to the publication, a private elevator landing opens onto the upper-level great room, where Davis kept his Steinway grand piano and hosted gatherings. At nearly 48 feet long, the room suggests an unusually generous setting for conversation and performance—not merely a place to arrange sofas.
A Different Register Downstairs

Robb Report places a formal dining room, a 12-seat Art Deco-style screening room and a larger secondary kitchen on the lower level, which has its own entrance. Editorially, that separation is the compelling move: dinner and a film have their own territory within the duplex.
Materials That Hold the Composition Together

The publication describes white oak herringbone-patterned floors alongside Macassar ebony paneling, cabinetry and bookcases. We love the contrast on paper: patterned oak and dark wood offer a decorative counterpoint to the home's expansive entertaining spaces, giving the feature a material story as well as a musical one.

item.title: A 1920s Seattle Tudor Blends Old-World Details With Modern Flourishes for $9.7 Million
item.summary: The Washington Park home features a stone arch the sellers won in a bidding war against Cher.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Seattle Tudor With a Collector’s Point of View
illustrationDraft.deck: A 1924 home in Washington Park pairs substantial proportions with European finds and an unusually rich palette of woodwork, according to Robb Report.
paragraphs: Scale with a historical anchor

Robb Report identifies the gated Tudor at 530 36th Avenue E as a five-bedroom, seven-bathroom residence spanning 7,910 square feet. Those are mansion-sized numbers, but the more compelling editorial thread is how a century-old architectural framework accommodates a distinctly personal collection.
A renovation built around discoveries

According to the publication, owners Jonathan and Elizabeth Roberts undertook a major remodeling between 2000 and 2004, incorporating pieces sourced across Europe. A stone archway from Ireland found its place in the gardens. To us, that intersection of architecture and collecting is the feature’s strongest idea: renovation as composition rather than wholesale replacement.
Woodwork supplies the continuity

The report describes hand-waxed woodwork in the main living areas, pecan floorboards in the dining room and a cherry-paneled office. Read together, those material choices suggest a useful counterpoint to the collected antiques—a shared vocabulary of timber rather than a succession of unrelated showpieces.
The landscape gets a final word

Robb Report also notes a half-moon bench overlooking the water, with the Cascades beyond, and a landscaped rooftop deck offering a broader view. The appeal is the contrast: rooms organized around crafted surfaces, followed by outdoor spaces whose principal subject is the landscape.

paragraphs: Scale With Structure

According to Robb Report, the retired quarterback acquired a roughly 8,700-square-foot residence on Palm Beach’s Billionaires Row. The publication describes five bedrooms across two levels. What interests us is how that generous scale accommodates distinct spaces for gathering and retreat, rather than relying on size alone.
A Rich Material Palette

Robb Report identifies imported French wooden inlay and marble floors, pecky cypress coffered ceilings, and French doors throughout. Those reported details suggest a design built around texture and craftsmanship. The contrast between patterned wood and stone gives the interiors a more specific identity than the mansion label conveys.
A Kitchen for Company

The kitchen includes a La Cornue range, a U-shaped island seating 10, and a breakfast nook, the publication reports. Editorially, that combination is compelling: it provides more than one setting for an informal meal, alongside the home’s separately reported formal dining room.
The Courtyard Counterpoint

Outside, Robb Report describes a central courtyard with a pool and spa beside an open-air loggia with a fireplace. That arrangement is the feature’s strongest counterpoint to the ornate interiors: an outdoor gathering space with its own architectural focus, not simply an expanse of lawn.

item.title: A Biotech Founder Is Asking $64 Million for His Brand-New Home on Florida’s Gulf Coast
item.summary: Poised to set a neighborhood record, the Barefoot Beach mansion has a rooftop pool and 120 feet of water frontage.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: Art and Water at Barefoot Beach
illustrationDraft.deck: A gallery-linked guest wing and a top-floor lap pool distinguish this Gulf-front Florida home.
paragraphs: Two waterfront connections

According to Robb Report, this four-story home in Barefoot Beach occupies roughly half an acre, with 120 feet of direct beachfront. The property also includes a canal-front boat slip and lift. For us, that combination is the waterfront story: the beach and boating each have a distinct place in the property’s design.
Art along the way

Robb Report describes a two-bedroom guest wing connected to the main house by an art gallery, with its own kitchen, living room and elevator. The appeal is architectural as much as decorative: a gallery turns the connection between shared and separate quarters into a space with a purpose of its own.
A top-floor departure

The publication places a 36-foot lap pool and spa on the top floor overlooking the Gulf, alongside a cabana and outdoor kitchen. That top-floor arrangement is the feature we find most distinctive. It gives swimming and outdoor entertaining an elevated setting rather than treating the pool as an automatic ground-level fixture.
Beyond the showpieces

Robb Report also details 103 support pilings, extensive waterproofing and drainage systems, and a whole-house backup generator. These reported specifications are not proof of storm-proof performance. They do, however, add a practical counterpoint to the gallery and pool—the less theatrical side of an unusually ambitious coastal home.
